edible.prep: Piñon nuts eaten raw, roasted, or ground into meal.

culture: Piñon nuts are a staple food across Nuche (Ute), Southern Paiute, Hopi, and Dine (Navajo) homelands, and piñon harvest remains a living seasonal practice, not a historical one. Pitch was worked as adhesive and as waterproofing for woven water bottles.
notes: Edible piñon seeds; cornerstone of pinyon-juniper woodland. CSU names pines among commonly ignitable natives — high resin content makes it ignitable regardless of irrigation. Keep out of HIZ 1–2.

soil: Wide range; very tolerant of poor, dry soil

edible.prep: Aromatic seed cones used sparingly as seasoning; more often steeped.

caution: Not a true berry. Avoid in pregnancy.
culture: Shredded juniper bark is worked into cordage, matting, tinder, and padding. The wood is rot-resistant and used for posts and bows. Juniper is burned ceremonially across the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau.
notes: CSU explicitly names junipers among the most ignitable natives — volatile oils burn hot even when well watered. Never plant within 30 ft of a structure. 'Woodward' is a Plant Select columnar form for high elevation.

edible.prep: Seed cones eaten in small quantity or ground into meal.

caution: Resinous; use sparingly.
culture: The defining tree of Colorado Plateau woodland economies. Bark is shredded for cordage, mats, and tinder; the durable wood is used for structures and tools.
notes: Dominant tree of Great Basin and Colorado Plateau woodlands. Picturesque multi-trunked form. Same ignitability caution as all junipers — HIZ 3 or beyond only.

edible.prep: Cambium peeled in spring and eaten fresh or dried.

caution: Peeling girdles and can kill young trees.
culture: Culturally scarred ponderosas -- trees bearing the peel scars of spring cambium harvest -- survive across Ute homelands in Colorado and are documented archaeological features. Some are over two centuries old. If a project site holds mature ponderosa, scarred trees are worth looking for before any clearing.
notes: Cinnamon bark with vanilla-butterscotch scent in heat. Thick bark is fire-adapted at the stand scale, but the crown is still ignitable near structures. Needs real space — 30 ft minimum.

edible.prep: Large seeds eaten raw or roasted.

culture: Seeds gathered as a supplemental nut crop at higher elevations where pinyon does not reach.
notes: Five-needle pine that goes higher than almost anything else. Flexible branches shed snow load; wind-sculpted at treeline. Excellent choice for exposed high-elevation sites well away from structures.
Extremely slow, extremely long-lived, sculptural. One of the few conifers genuinely at home above 9,000 ft. Resents rich soil and irrigation. Specimen use — its form is the whole point.

soil: Moist, well-drained; dislikes hot dry clay

edible.prep: Cambium scraped and eaten in spring.

culture: Inner bark harvested as a spring food; the light wood worked for containers and utensils. Note that the carved aspens most common in Colorado today are Basque sheepherder arborglyphs from the early 1900s, a separate history worth not conflating.
notes: CSU's go-to fire-resistant deciduous tree for mountain properties — high leaf moisture, low resin, and no canopy fuel when dormant. Clonal; expect suckers. Not truly xeric — wants supplemental water on dry sites.

edible.prep: Boiled down as a sweetener, in the manner of sugar maple.

notes: The West's answer to sugar maple — canyon-slope native with red-orange-yellow fall color. CSU rates maples as fire-resistant deciduous choices. Far more drought-tolerant than eastern maples.

culture: Hard, straight-grained wood worked for bows, snowshoe frames, and implement handles.
notes: Multi-stemmed understory maple for shadier, moister mountain sites. Good fire-resistant screening near structures. Handles more elevation than bigtooth maple. CORRECTED 2026-08 - was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 6 (p.14). Below 8, so out of HIZ 1-2. FireSmart BC independently places Acer glabrum in its Extended Zone (10-30 m) and flags it 'more research required, use with caution' - two sources, neither Colorado, agreeing it does not belong near a structure.

soil: Wide range; tolerates rocky and clay

edible.prep: Leached to remove tannins, then ground into meal.

caution: Must be leached; raw acorns are astringent and hard on the gut.
culture: Gambel oak mast was a significant fall resource in Nuche territory, and remains critical to bear, deer, and turkey. The hard wood is used for tools and fuel.
notes: CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU names Gambel oak among Colorado's commonly ignitable shrubs. Dense rhizomatous thickets carry fire readily. Ecologically invaluable (acorn mast, cover) but keep it out of HIZ 1–2 and break up continuity.

edible.prep: Whole cherries pounded pit-and-all, dried into cakes, and mixed with fat and meat for pemmican.

caution: Leaves, twigs, and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides. Traditional preparation involves drying, which reduces them. Do not present raw pits as food.
culture: One of the most important fruits in the northern and central Rockies. The whole-fruit pounding method -- pits included -- is the traditional preparation and distinguishes it from how settlers used chokecherry. Straight stems worked for arrow shafts.
notes: Fragrant white flower racemes, dark astringent fruit used for jelly and syrup. Suckers into thickets. Foliage and pits contain cyanogenic compounds — note near livestock. CORRECTED 2026-08 - was ign 8 (estimated); it is not a fire-resistant screen. Idaho Firewise rates it twice and inconsistently: 5 in the shrub chapter (p.52) and 6 in the deciduous tree chapter (p.58), same dimensions in both. Taking the lower reading as the conservative one for a safety field. Either way it is out of HIZ 1-2.

culture: The wood is dense enough to sink in water and is worked into digging sticks, arrow shafts, and tool handles -- the reason for the 'mahogany' name, which has nothing to do with true mahogany. Root and bark yield a red-brown dye.
notes: CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU lists mountain mahogany among commonly ignitable natives. Evergreen, long-lived, actinorhizal nitrogen fixer. Twisted feathery seed plumes. Critical winter browse. Site in HIZ 3.

caution: Volatile oils; not a culinary sage. Do not substitute for Salvia officinalis.
culture: Bark is stripped and worked into cordage, matting, and woven sandals. Sagebrush is burned ceremonially across the Great Basin. This is Artemisia, not Salvia -- the 'sage' in sagebrush is a settler misnaming that persists in nursery trade.
notes: The defining shrub of the Intermountain West. Volatile terpenes make it burn explosively — among the most ignitable things you can plant. Irreplaceable for sage-obligate wildlife, but HIZ 3 and beyond only.

caution: Volatile oils.
culture: Used ceremonially and as a steeped beverage across the Plains and Great Basin. Often gathered where big sagebrush does not grow.
notes: Fine silver-white filigree foliage, semi-woody subshrub. Far lower fuel volume than big sagebrush but still aromatic and resinous. Excellent silver textural filler on lean, dry ground.

culture: A major dye plant. The flowering heads yield yellows through olive-golds and are central to Dine (Navajo) weaving. Latex in the stems was chewed as gum, and the species was investigated as a domestic rubber source during both World Wars.
notes: Golden September bloom when almost nothing else is flowering — a genuinely important late-season nectar source. Resinous stems raise ignitability. Cut back hard in spring to keep it dense and reduce dead fuel.

culture: Yields yellow dye in the same manner as rubber rabbitbrush, though less commonly used.
notes: Smaller, tidier cousin of rubber rabbitbrush with sticky green stems. Better scaled for residential beds. Same resin caution — keep it out of the first 30 ft.

edible.prep: Seeds eaten; bitter foliage is not a food.

caution: Foliage intensely bitter -- the common name is literal.
notes: Arguably the single most important mule deer browse shrub in the West. Actinorhizal nitrogen fixer. Small fragrant yellow flowers. Resents irrigation and clay — give it coarse ground and walk away.

edible.prep: Tart red berries steeped in cold water for a beverage; also dried and ground.

culture: The premier basketry material of the Great Basin and Southwest. Young stems are split and coiled for baskets across Nuche, Southern Paiute, Dine, and Puebloan traditions -- fine coiled work depends on it. Berries make a tart cold-steeped drink; foliage and fruit yield black dye and act as mordant.
notes: CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU names three-leaf sumac among commonly ignitable shrubs. The straight species belongs in HIZ 3. Note: the low cultivar 'Autumn Amber' IS rated 8 by CSU and is fine near structures. Superb fall color; tart edible berries.

edible.prep: Same tart berries as the species.

culture: A modern ornamental selection of the same species used for basketry, though its prostrate habit does not produce the long straight stems that split well.
notes: Prostrate New Mexico selection — a groundcover version of skunkbush at roughly a foot tall and eight feet wide. CSU rates it 8, so unlike the species it can go inside 30 ft. Brilliant amber-red fall color.

edible.prep: Berries steeped for a tart cold beverage.

culture: Berries cold-steeped as a drink; leaves dried and added to smoking mixtures. Bark and fruit yield dyes ranging tan through black.
notes: Rated 8 by CSU — acceptable near structures, unlike its three-leaf relative. Scarlet fall color and persistent red fruit clusters. Suckers aggressively; give it room or plan to manage the colony edge.

edible.prep: Eaten fresh, or dried and pounded into cakes; a core pemmican fruit.

culture: Among the most important fruits across the northern Rockies and Plains. Dried serviceberry cakes stored through winter, and the fruit is a defining pemmican ingredient alongside chokecherry. Saskatoon, the Canadian city, takes its name from the Cree word for this fruit.
notes: CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU rates Utah serviceberry 7.5, just BELOW the 8-point threshold for the first 30 ft. Still a top-tier plant: earliest bloom, best native fruit, strong fall color. Just site it past HIZ 2.

culture: Same dense wood and red-brown root dye as curlleaf mountain mahogany, and worked for the same digging sticks and shafts.
notes: CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU lists mountain mahogany among commonly ignitable natives. Deciduous counterpart to curlleaf. Silvery twisted seed tails catch low autumn light. Excellent on rocky cut slopes, in HIZ 3.

culture: Straight young stems worked for arrow shafts and bound into brooms.
notes: White rose-like flowers and pink feathery seed plumes on the plant simultaneously, for months. Semi-evergreen with fine twiggy stems — the twigginess is what holds its rating down. Backlight it.
Aromatic fern-like evergreen foliage with white flower spikes in midsummer — an underused Great Basin native. Resinous and aromatic, so treat it like sagebrush for siting. Superb in gravel gardens.

edible.prep: Seeds ground into meal; young greens cooked.

caution: Accumulates salts and selenium from soil; leaves are salty by nature.
culture: The ash of burned saltbush is used as leavening and as the colorant that gives Hopi and Dine blue corn breads their color -- a genuinely surprising use for a plant most people read as roadside scrub.
notes: Family corrected to Amaranthaceae (Chenopodiaceae is sunk under APG IV). CSU notes salt-tolerant plants tend to resist ignition — saltbush is a rare xeric shrub that's both very low water and fire-defensible. Papery four-winged seeds persist. CORRECTED 2026-08 - was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 6 (p.12). Below 8, so out of HIZ 1-2. Not listed by FireSmart BC, so Idaho is the only source here.

soil: Alkaline, clay to sandy; salt tolerant
notes: Woolly white seed heads glow when backlit through late fall and winter — the reason to plant it. Exceptional winter forage protein. Nomenclature is a mess; order by any of three names.

caution: Berries are widely considered inedible and are emetic in quantity. Do not present as food.
culture: Straight stems worked for arrow shafts and pipe stems. The white berries are a wildlife food, not a human one -- worth stating plainly on any plant list a homeowner will read.
notes: CSU rates Symphoricarpos 8 — one of the few natives genuinely suited to the first 30 ft. Waxy white berries persist into winter. Thicket-forming; excellent erosion control on disturbed mountain slopes.

edible.prep: Tart berries eaten fresh or made into jelly.

culture: The root's inner bark is brilliant yellow with berberine and yields a strong yellow dye used for basketry materials, leather, and textiles. Tart berries make excellent jelly. A dye plant hiding in plain sight as a shade groundcover.
notes: Name updated — POWO accepts Berberis repens; nurseries still list Mahonia. Evergreen holly-like groundcover shrub for dry shade under conifers, a genuinely hard niche to fill. Foliage turns burgundy in winter.
look: A low, spreading evergreen shrub of glossy, spiny holly-like leaflets that bronze in cold, with clusters of small yellow flowers followed by dusty-blue berries.

edible.prep: Eaten fresh, or dried for storage.

culture: Currants dried and stored for winter across the Great Basin and Rockies. The clove-scented bloom is an early marker in the seasonal round.
notes: Clove-scented golden flowers among the first nectar of the season. Edible berries ripen amber to black. Deciduous with high leaf moisture — a reasonable choice closer in. Check local white pine blister rust rules before specifying Ribes. CORRECTED 2026-08 - was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 6 (p.14). Below 8, so out of HIZ 1-2. FireSmart BC lists no Ribes aureum; its other currants sit at Extended or 'more research'. Genus-level only, so not treated as corroboration.

edible.prep: Hips eaten fresh or steeped; very high in vitamin C.

caution: Strain the irritating seed hairs before consuming.
culture: Rose hips are a reliable late-season vitamin C source that persists on the plant through winter, making them available when little else is.
notes: Fragrant pink single flowers, then orange-red hips that hold all winter. Suckers into thickets — use it where you want a wildlife hedgerow, not a tidy bed. Very tolerant of a wide moisture range.

edible.prep: Berries whipped with water into a foam -- saponins act as the whipping agent.

caution: Saponins cause GI upset in quantity. Bitter by nature.
culture: The saponin content that makes these berries bitter also lets them whip like egg white, producing the foamed dish widely known as 'Indian ice cream' across the northern Rockies and interior Northwest. It is still made.
notes: Actinorhizal nitrogen fixer with olive-green leaves silvered beneath. Dioecious — you need both sexes for fruit. Extremely cold hardy; one of the better shrubs above 9,000 ft.

soil: Very adaptable; tolerates clay and alkaline
notes: Fast, tough, and takes hard shearing — the best native hedge or windbreak option for the region. Blue-black fruit on female plants draws birds. Deciduous with good moisture content. Elevation ceiling around 7,500 ft.

culture: Leaves and flowers lather in water as a soap. The straight hard stems are worked for arrow shafts, bows, and pipe stems -- the reason for the old name 'arrowwood'. Idaho's state flower.
notes: Intensely fragrant white June flowers — the scent carries across a yard. CSU rates it 8, so it works close to the house. 'Cheyenne' is the regional selection. Idaho's state flower.

Compact native ninebark for rocky mountain slopes and part shade. Exfoliating bark gives winter interest; rosy fall color. Much better adapted to high elevation than the common eastern P. opulifolius cultivars.

soil: Rocky, well-drained; cliff and canyon native
notes: Plant Select, trialed successfully at 8,150 ft. Waxy white flower clusters, felted blue-green leaves, and reliable orange-red fall color. A true Colorado cliff native — outstanding in rock work and on north-facing slopes.

Plant Select high-altitude pick. True legume nitrogen fixer with fine pinnate foliage and dense purple flower spikes loaded with orange anthers. Small enough for residential beds; tolerates real neglect.

culture: Stems are hard and straight enough that the genus is called 'ironwood' or 'arrowwood' in places; worked for arrow shafts, digging sticks, and pins.
notes: Creamy plumes age to russet and hold through winter — one of the best dried-structure shrubs in the flora. Native to rock outcrops and canyon walls, so it's ideal draping over boulder walls and retaining structures.

edible.prep: Eaten fresh or dried; also pounded into cakes.

caution: Pits contain cyanogenic glycosides like other Prunus.
culture: A significant Plains and foothills fruit, dried and stored in the same manner as chokecherry.
notes: 'Pawnee Buttes' is the low spreading Plant Select form (about 18 in tall) — excellent on slopes and wall tops. White spring bloom, edible black fruit, burgundy fall color. Deciduous and fire-defensible. CORRECTED 2026-08 - was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 6 (p.14). Below 8, so out of HIZ 1-2. FireSmart BC lists Prunus besseyi under 'more research required, use with caution', which supports keeping it away from structures without giving a number.

Plant Select, trialed at 8,150 ft. Evergreen with mahogany bark and pink urn flowers — better adapted to Colorado alkalinity than A. uva-ursi. 'Panchito' and 'Chieftain' are the named forms. Deer will browse it. Waxy evergreen leaves are moderately ignitable.

caution: Saponins -- lathering does not mean edible.
culture: Leaves and flowers lather readily in water and are used as a soap and hair wash; also steeped as a beverage. The Ceanothus genus is a widespread soap plant across the West.
notes: Glossy resin-varnished evergreen leaves that smell like balsam — and burn like it. A genuine fire-cycle species whose seed germinates after heat scarification. Nitrogen fixing and ecologically valuable, but among the worst choices near a structure.

edible.prep: Stems steeped for a beverage known as Mormon tea or Brigham tea.

caution: Contains ephedrine-type alkaloids. Ephedra is federally regulated as a dietary supplement ingredient. Do not present preparation instructions or health claims.
culture: Steeped green stems make the beverage settlers named Mormon tea, a use adopted from Southern Paiute, Nuche, and Puebloan practice. Handle this one carefully in writing -- the alkaloid content puts it under federal supplement regulation.
notes: REVISED FROM v1 — CSU rates Ephedra 8, and lists green photosynthetic stems as an ignition-RESISTANT trait. My v1 'Low' rating was wrong. Architectural jointed broom-like form, striking in gravel gardens. Slow.

edible.prep: Pads (nopales) singed to remove spines then roasted; fruit (tunas) eaten fresh or dried.

caution: Glochids -- the fine hairlike spines -- are the real hazard, not the large spines. Site away from paths and pets.
culture: Both pads and fruit are eaten across the Southwest and Great Basin, with spines burned off before preparation. Prickly pear is also the single least ignitable plant on the CSU list, which makes it a rare case where the fire story and the food story point the same direction.
notes: CSU rates Opuntia a perfect 10 — the least ignitable plant on their entire list, and pictured on the fact sheet cover. Enormous silky yellow-to-pink flowers. Note glochids near walkways. Absolutely no supplemental water once established.

edible.prep: Sweet fruit eaten fresh.

caution: Spines.
culture: The fruit is sweet and was gathered where the plant is locally abundant, though the species is too scattered to be a staple.
notes: Waxy scarlet cups that stay open for days — the finest hummingbird cactus in the flora, and hardy remarkably high. Forms slow mounding clumps. Needs sharp drainage and a warm exposure; rot is the only real risk.

edible.prep: Flower buds pit-roasted; fruit eaten.

caution: Detached joints root readily and the spines are barbed.
culture: Buds pit-roasted as a food across the southern Colorado Plateau. The woody lattice skeleton is worked decoratively.
notes: Sculptural branching form with magenta flowers and persistent yellow fruit; the lattice skeleton is ornamental after death. Detached joints root readily — site it well away from paths and pets.

edible.prep: Flower stalks and buds roasted; fruit eaten.

caution: Root saponins are not edible.
culture: The whole plant is a toolkit: saponin-rich roots pounded for soap and shampoo, leaf fiber stripped for cordage, sandals, nets, and mats, and stalks and fruit eaten. 'Soapweed' is a direct translation of the use. Yucca also depends entirely on yucca moths for pollination -- a mutualism worth telling clients about.
notes: CSU rates it 8 — a bold evergreen accent that's fine near structures. Obligate mutualism with yucca moths, so it's a real ecological choice, not just a form choice. Saponin-rich roots were traditional soap. Hardiest yucca in the region.

edible.prep: Thick fleshy fruit eaten fresh, roasted, or dried and pressed into cakes.

caution: Root saponins are not edible.
culture: The best-eating yucca fruit in the region -- thick and sweet, dried into storable cakes. Same root soap and leaf fiber uses as soapweed. Central to Puebloan, Dine, and Southern Paiute plant economies.
notes: Broader, bluer, and coarser than soapweed, with thick fleshy edible fruit. Heavier textural mass — use it as a single specimen rather than in repetition. Same yucca moth relationship.

edible.prep: Succulent leaves eaten raw or cooked as a green.

caution: Mildly astringent raw.
culture: Eaten as a fresh green at elevations where few other greens grow -- one of the few edible plants on this list that reaches treeline.
notes: Rated 10 by CSU. Native alpine stonecrop that goes to 12,000 ft — one of very few things on this list genuinely at home at treeline. Yellow star flowers over succulent rosettes that redden in cold. Ideal for green roofs and rock crevices.

soil: Well-drained; tolerates clay better than most penstemons
notes: Height corrected to 2–2.5 ft per CSU. The most reliable and forgiving xeric penstemon — the one to use when a planting has to succeed. Deep blue-violet spikes; pictured in the CSU fact sheet. Good to 10,000 ft.
Pure scarlet tubes timed to hummingbird migration — one of the earliest significant nectar sources in the region. Needs sharp drainage; short-lived in heavy soil but self-sows.

The only fragrant penstemon, and the tallest — five-foot spires of inflated pale pink flowers. Short-lived but self-sows freely. Standard in western roadside reclamation mixes for exactly that reason.

Plant Select, trialed at 8,150 ft. Needle-fine evergreen foliage in low mounds with orange-red tubes over a long season. 'Half Pint' is compact; 'Sunset Glow' is the newer SteppeSuns selection. Longer-lived than most penstemons.
Ground-hugging blue-flowered mat, listed by CSU to 10,000 ft. 'Waggon Wheel' is the Plant Select form. Use it as a flowering alternative to thyme between flagstones in high-elevation work.
Glaucous blue-gray foliage with lavender-pink flowers held to one side of the stem. Foliage color alone earns it a spot. Foothills to montane; wants lean, gravelly ground.

edible.prep: Leaves and flowers steeped as a beverage.

culture: Steeped as a beverage and used medicinally across the Great Basin. Buckwheats are also among the highest-value specialist bee plants in the flora, which is the stronger story for a pollinator-focused design.
notes: Sulfur umbels age through orange to deep rust and hold for months. Host plant for numerous specialist bees and blue butterflies — one of the highest-value pollinator plants here. 'Kannah Creek' is the Plant Select form, good to 8,150 ft.

edible.prep: Steeped as a beverage.

culture: Used as a steeped beverage and medicinally in the southern Rockies.
notes: Creamy-white to pale yellow umbels over felted gray-green basal mats. Later and softer than sulphur buckwheat — pair the two to extend buckwheat bloom across the whole season.

soil: Lean, well-drained; poor soil is fine
notes: Height revised to 1–1.5 ft per CSU. Blooms from June to frost — the longest season of any native here. Deadhead for more, or leave seed heads for goldfinches. Rich soil makes it floppy and short-lived.

caution: Contains thujone. Not for internal use without guidance.
culture: One of the most widely used medicinal plants in North America -- documented across a remarkable number of nations, primarily as a wound and fever herb. The genus name honors Achilles, who is said to have carried it for battle wounds; the plant's reputation crosses continents.
notes: Rated 9.5 by CSU — one of the highest-scoring perennials available, and a top pick for the first five feet from a structure. Spreads by rhizome; use where that's an asset. Feathery foliage, flat white umbels.

edible.prep: Seeds eaten parched or ground.

caution: Raw seed contains trace cyanogenic compounds; parching addresses this.
culture: This is flax. Stems yield strong bast fiber worked into cordage, fishing line, nets, and snares across the Great Basin and Plateau -- the same fiber tradition as Old World flax, arrived at independently. Named for Meriwether Lewis, who collected it in 1806.
notes: Sky-blue flowers open at dawn and drop by afternoon, replaced daily for weeks. Airy enough to weave through everything else. Short-lived but self-sows reliably — treat it as a matrix species, not a specimen.

caution: Star-shaped leaf hairs irritate skin and eyes. Wear gloves.
culture: Mucilaginous tissue used as a poultice. The Hopi name translates roughly to a plant of gladness. Its stronger design story is ecological: it supports globemallow bees, which visit almost nothing else.
notes: Apricot-orange mallow cups over silver-hairy foliage. Supports globemallow bees (Diadasia), which visit almost nothing else. Rhizomatous — it wanders. Star-shaped leaf hairs can irritate skin; wear gloves.

edible.prep: Deep taproot roasted and eaten.

culture: The large taproot was dug and roasted on the Plains -- worth knowing that harvesting it kills the plant, which is also why mature specimens transplant so poorly.
notes: Magenta chalices on trailing stems that sprawl over walls and edges. Deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought-proof once established — and makes transplanting mature plants a losing proposition. Site it once.

edible.prep: Flower heads and leaves steeped as a beverage.

culture: Steeped as a beverage by Lakota and Cheyenne among others; the flower heads also yield a yellow-orange dye.
notes: Tall thimble-shaped cones with reflexed yellow or mahogany rays that move in any breeze. Self-sows into drifts — ideal in seeded meadow work, less so in tightly controlled beds.

caution: Do not present preparation or dosage. Wild populations are seriously depleted by overharvest.
culture: The most significant medicinal plant of the Plains, and the species behind the modern echinacea supplement trade -- which has driven serious wild overharvest. Planting the true narrow-leaf species in gardens is a small counterweight worth naming in a post.
notes: The genuinely xeric coneflower — far better adapted to dry western soils than the E. purpurea cultivars sold everywhere. Slower to establish because it builds a taproot first. Leave seed heads for winter structure and finches.

Chronically overlooked and hard to kill. Silvery hairy foliage with golden daisies from midsummer to frost, on soils where little else will hold. Use it as a workhorse filler in reclamation and roadside work.

CSU lists it to 10,000 ft. Smooth blue-green foliage and clouds of lavender-blue daisies in September, when late pollinators most need forage. Pair with rabbitbrush and goldenrod for a full fall nectar sequence.
Plant Select alpine goldenrod, compact and non-aggressive unlike the tall spreading species. Trialed at 8,150 ft and native well above that. Goldenrod does not cause hay fever — that's ragweed.

caution: Contains quinolizidine alkaloids and is toxic to livestock and people. Not a food. Seedpods have been mistaken for edible legumes.
culture: Worth flagging on any planting list precisely because it looks like a pea and is not. The yellow bloom is one of the earliest strong colors in the mountain spring.
notes: Yellow lupine-like spikes in May, well before most natives start. True legume nitrogen fixer. Rhizomatous and genuinely aggressive — deploy it for slope stabilization and naturalized areas, not refined borders.

edible.prep: Nectar spurs sipped by children in many traditions.

caution: Foliage and seed contain cardiogenic toxins. Only the nectar spur, and only in trace amounts.
culture: Sipping nectar from the spurs is a near-universal childhood practice wherever columbines grow. That is the extent of its food use -- the rest of the plant is not edible.
notes: Long-spurred yellow flowers over a remarkably long season. 'Denver Gold' is the Plant Select form, trialed at 8,150 ft. More sun- and drought-tolerant than blue columbine, though it still wants more water than true xerics.

edible.prep: Young leaves and roots eaten.

culture: Leaves and roots eaten as a minor food across its enormous circumboreal range -- the same species grows in Scotland, where it is the bluebell of song.
notes: Rated 9.5 by CSU and listed blooming May through October — an unusually long season for a native. Nodding blue bells on wiry stems that thread through rock work. Circumboreal; equally at home in Scotland and at 11,000 ft here.

edible.prep: Mustard-family seeds and young greens eaten; seeds ground.

caution: Pungent.
culture: Seeds ground into meal and greens eaten in spring across the Great Basin and Southwest, in the manner of other wild mustards.
notes: Rated 9 by CSU. Dense heads of fragrant yellow-orange flowers on erect stems. Biennial to short-lived perennial — let it seed itself around. Pictured in the CSU fact sheet alongside penstemons.

Plant Select, trialed at 8,150 ft. Fluorescent orange-scarlet trumpets in August and September — precisely timed to southbound hummingbird migration, when little else is blooming. Low spreading mat. Slow to emerge in spring; don't assume it's dead.

caution: Root contains active compounds; not a food.
culture: The large tuberous root has documented ceremonial and medicinal use in the Southwest. Its design story is better told through the hawkmoths -- the flowers open at dusk specifically for them.
notes: Magenta trumpets open late afternoon and hold through the night for hawkmoths — one of the few nocturnal-pollinator plants worth designing around. Builds an enormous tuber; a mature plant can mound six feet across. Very late to emerge.

Yellow daisies that smell distinctly of cocoa in the early morning, fading by midday. Site it along a walk or near a patio where people pass before nine. Green cup-shaped bracts persist after petals drop.

Low rhizomatous mat smothered in papery yellow daisies for months, aging to straw and holding through winter. Among the most drought-proof groundcovers available. Slow to establish, then indestructible.

edible.prep: Taproot cooked and eaten.

culture: The thick taproot eaten as a cooked root vegetable on the southern Plains.
notes: Enormous lemon-yellow cups — four inches across on a foot-tall plant — opening at dusk. Large winged seed pods afterward are ornamental in their own right. Taprooted; site it permanently.

caution: Toxic raw. Contains cardiac glycosides. Do not present as food. Historically called pleurisy root.
culture: Widely used medicinally on the Plains under the name pleurisy root. Milkweed stems in the broader genus are a major cordage fiber. Its strongest story now is monarch host plant -- and this species blooms below about 6,500 ft, so check elevation before promising monarchs.
notes: Monarch host plant with brilliant orange umbels. CSU lists its elevation range as roughly 5,000–6,500 ft, so it's marginal in the high mountain valleys — verify before specifying above 7,000 ft. Very late to emerge; mark its location.

edible.prep: Roots steeped as a beverage with a root-beer note.

culture: Roots steeped for a beverage described as tasting of sassafras or root beer -- the plant is sometimes called old man's whiskers for the seed plumes.
notes: Nodding dusky-pink bells give way to smoky feathered seed plumes that are the real show, lasting weeks. Semi-evergreen ferny basal foliage reddens in fall. Listed by CSU to 10,000 ft.

soil: Gritty, sharply drained; no clay, no irrigation

edible.prep: Leaves steeped as a beverage.

caution: Strongly aromatic; volatile oils.
culture: Steeped as a beverage and used ceremonially across the Great Basin. Unlike sagebrush, this genuinely is a Salvia.
notes: Electric violet-blue flowers with rosy bracts over silver-white foliage — arguably the most striking color combination in the Great Basin flora. Aromatic oils raise ignitability. Crown rot in any heavy or wet soil; give it pure grit.

soil: Sharply drained; wet winter soil kills it

edible.prep: Leaves and flowers steeped as a beverage.

culture: Steeped for a mint-family beverage; the bubblegum scent of the foliage is unusually strong for the genus.
notes: Rose-pink spikes from July to frost with foliage that smells like bubblegum. A major late-season hummingbird plant. Aromatic oils raise ignitability modestly. Winter drainage matters more than cold hardiness — most losses are rot, not freeze.

caution: Astringent.
culture: Heuchera roots are strongly astringent, which is the origin of the common name alum root, and were used to treat wounds and sores.
notes: Plant Select, trialed at 8,150 ft. Dwarf New Mexico native with rose-pink flower wands over neat evergreen rosettes. Far more drought- and sun-tolerant than the foliage-hybrid heucheras. Ideal in wall crevices and shaded rock work.
look: Neat rosettes of small scalloped green leaves, with slender wiry wands of tiny rose-pink bell flowers held above them.

notes: Plant Select 'Rambler', trialed at 8,150 ft. Lavender-blue daisies with yellow centers over a long midsummer season. A high-elevation native that reads as a refined garden perennial — useful when a design needs polish above 8,000 ft.

Rated 9 by CSU as a turf grass. Eyelash seed heads held horizontally. The premier low-water lawn alternative — mow to 4 in for turf, or leave unmown as a meadow matrix. Warm-season; greens up late. CSU caps it near 7,500 ft.

Rated 9 by CSU. Sod-forming by stolons, so it makes a true walkable lawn unlike bunch-forming blue grama. Warm-season and dormant tan for much of the year. CSU caps it around 6,500 ft — too low for most mountain valleys.
Oat-like seed spikelets dangle along one side of arching stems, with purple anthers at bloom. Taller architecture than blue grama for the middle layer. Host plant for several skipper butterflies.

syn: Achnatherum hymenoides, Stipa hymenoides, Oryzopsis hymenoides
soil: Sandy, gravelly, sharply drained; no wet soil

edible.prep: Seeds parched and ground into flour or meal.

caution: Ergot can occur on grass seed heads; harvest clean.
culture: One of the most important wild grains of the Great Basin -- seeds parched and ground into flour, and specifically valued as a food that carried people through drought years when other crops failed. It is the state grass of Utah for exactly this reason.
notes: Nomenclature is genuinely unsettled — POWO accepts Eriocoma, USDA PLANTS still uses Achnatherum, Calflora uses Stipa. Order under all three. Airy cloud-like panicles that catch light better than any other regional grass. Utah's state grass. Won't tolerate poor drainage. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 1 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 (30-100 ft) — the lowest grass rating in the database, alongside needle-and-thread. The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2. Idaho lists it as Achnatherum hymenoides.

edible.prep: Seeds parched and ground.

caution: The sharp awns injure eyes, mouths, and paws -- pets and livestock.
culture: Seeds gathered and ground as a minor grain. The self-drilling awn is one of the more remarkable mechanisms in the flora and makes good content on its own.
notes: Long twisting awns hygroscopically drill seed into the soil as humidity changes — a genuinely remarkable mechanism. Cool-season, so it's green early when warm-season grasses are still dormant. Awns can injure pets and livestock. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 1 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 (30-100 ft) — the lowest grass rating in the database, alongside Indian ricegrass. The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2.

Fine blue-green semi-evergreen bunchgrass — the best textural counterpoint to coarse shrubs and yuccas. Cool-season; may go summer-dormant in heat. Handles considerably more elevation than blue grama. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 9 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 6 (p.15), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho's 6 is annotated as assuming moderate summer irrigation; unirrigated and summer-dormant it will behave worse. The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2.

Tight silvery-green spike-like panicles in June, well before other grasses flower. Cool-season, compact, and unusually tolerant of high elevation. An underused matrix grass for mountain meadow plantings. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 9 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 4 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 (30-100 ft). The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2.

Strongly rhizomatous blue-gray cool-season grass — the workhorse for erosion control and reclamation on heavy alkaline clay where almost nothing else establishes. Too aggressive for ornamental beds; use it as a functional groundplane. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 4 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 and notes explicitly that it “creates a continuous fuel” — the rhizomatous habit that makes it useful for reclamation is what carries fire. The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2. Idaho lists it as Agropyron smithii.

Blue-green summer foliage turning copper-orange in fall and holding that color all winter — the best cool-season color payoff of any regional grass. Warm-season. Rich soil or irrigation makes it flop; keep it lean. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 3 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 (30-100 ft). The winter colour that makes it ornamental is cured standing fuel. The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2.

edible.prep: Abundant fine seed parched and ground into flour.

culture: Dropseed produces prodigious quantities of fine seed, gathered and ground into flour across the Southwest and southern Plains. A famine-year staple.
notes: Pioneer species that establishes fast on raw sandy ground — a reclamation standby. Fine open panicles partly enclosed in the leaf sheath. Warm-season. Best used functionally rather than as a specimen. CORRECTED 2026-08 — was ign 8 (estimated). Idaho Firewise master database rates it 4 (p.17), filing it under non-turf grasses. Idaho places it in Zone 3 (30-100 ft). The previous estimate generalised from CSU's turf-grass ratings (blue grama 9, buffalograss 9), which describe short irrigated lawn grasses, not a bunchgrass that cures. Keep out of HIZ 1-2.

Fine-textured bunchgrass with pinkish-purple fall inflorescence. Native to high montane meadows and ponderosa understory, so it's one of the better ornamental grasses above 8,000 ft. Rarely offered — source it early.

WATER CORRECTED FROM v1 — CSU lists water needs as Medium, not Very Low. My v1 rating was too dry. Silver-gray stoloniferous mat with fuzzy white flower heads. Host plant for American lady butterflies. Listed to 10,000 ft.

soil: Gravelly, sharply drained; no wet feet
notes: Tight cushion buried under white to lavender flowers for two weeks in early spring, then a neutral gray-green mat the rest of the season. Wants pure grit — the fastest way to kill it is irrigation.

Silver-felted rosettes with cream to rose pompom heads on short stalks. Alpine-adapted to 11,000 ft — one of the highest-elevation options here. Strictly for rock gardens, crevices, and gravel; no clay, no water.

Evergreen mat that grips bare rock and limestone cliffs, with tiny bottlebrush flower spikes in midsummer. The specialist choice for dry stone wall faces and boulder crevices where soil is essentially absent.

Fine-textured evergreen for dry shade beneath conifers — one of very few natives that genuinely performs there. Inconspicuous flowers; grown entirely for the glossy foliage mass. Waxy evergreen leaves keep the rating middling.

soil: Acidic, well-drained; struggles in alkaline soil

edible.prep: Dried leaves smoked, usually blended with tobacco or bearberry bark.

caution: Berries are dry and mealy; edible but poor.
culture: The name kinnikinnick is Algonquian and means, roughly, 'smoking mixture' -- the plant is named for the use. Dried leaves are blended into smoking mixtures across a huge swath of the continent. The most literally named plant in this database.
notes: Evergreen mat with pink urn flowers and red berries. Note the real limitation: it wants acidic soil and often sulks in Colorado's alkaline ground — Arctostaphylos × coloradensis is the better regional choice. Waxy leaves are moderately ignitable.

Plant Select, trialed at 8,150 ft. Glossy evergreen mat that disappears under true-blue flowers in April and May. Takes light foot traffic — the best non-native between-pavers plant for high elevation. Not invasive in this region.

edible.prep: Culinary herb.

culture: An Old World culinary and medicinal herb with a long Mediterranean and European history -- worth distinguishing from the native plants here rather than folding into the same story.
notes: CSU rates 'Minus' at 8 and lists it to 10,000 ft. Aromatic mat that tolerates light foot traffic and swarms with bees in bloom. Non-native but well-behaved. Shear after flowering to keep it dense and reduce dead thatch.

soil: Sharply drained; winter wet is fatal
notes: Rated 10 by CSU — succulent leaves make it among the most ignition-resistant plants available, and it's pictured on the fact sheet. Note the elevation ceiling: CSU and Pueblo Extension both cap D. cooperi near 6,000 ft, so it's marginal in mountain valleys. Hardier Delosperma species go higher.

Reads as drift rather than specimen — wiry stems hold single yellow heads above thin foliage. Rated Very Low water on the Fort Collins list; carries Xerces Society 'special value to native bees'. Varieties multiflora (Rocky Mountain states) and nevadensis (southwest) both occur in Colorado. Bloom window differs by source: Fort Collins May-Sep, Wildflower Center Jul-Oct. Field note: wild drift on a dry roadside cut at 8,634 ft, Eagle County, 2026-08-15.

Rhizomatous spreader. NRCS lists it for revegetation of disturbed areas, mine spoil reclamation and soil stabilization, and explicitly notes it is not typically planted in a landscape setting due to its spreading rhizomatous growth. Specify it for cut banks and disturbed ground, not borders. Distinct from #65 S. multiradiata, the compact non-aggressive Plant Select alpine goldenrod.

Colorado native (var. incisum), rated Very Low water on the Fort Collins plant list. Upright bushy clump 1-3 ft tall by 1.5-2 ft wide; sticky glandular hairs on stems and leaves give it its name. Blooms June through August, foliage turns red in fall. An important larval and adult food host for many native invertebrates. Field note: found wild on a ski slope at 7,876 ft, Eagle County.

soil: Well-drained; tolerates clay, loam or sand
notes: Grassy clump 2-3 ft tall and wide with bicolor spikes to 2-4 ft total. Exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, though it appreciates deep watering during bloom and extended dry spells. In zones 4-6 the foliage may need tying over the crown so water does not pool and freeze on it. Field note, Eagle County ~7,150 ft: performs in full sun on low water and high heat, but river-rock mulch banked extra heat around the crown — a real tradeoff, not a pure upside.

soil: Moist gritty loam in spring, dry in summer dormancy
notes: Spring ephemeral from a deep corm — flowers with the snowmelt under aspen and spruce, then goes fully dormant by midsummer. One of very few genuinely shade-tolerant species in this database, and CSU rates it 9.5. Site it where summer dormancy will not read as a hole: through a groundcover, or under deciduous shrubs.

Frothy white panicles over whorled leaves, circumboreal and thoroughly at home in mountain shade. Rhizomatous — specify for bank stabilisation, woodland edge and naturalised areas, not for a mixed border where it will run through its neighbours.

Nodding blue bells opening from pink buds, the earliest substantial bloom in a mountain garden. CSU rates it 10 — the highest available — and it takes shade as readily as sun, which is a rare combination here.
Magenta-veined pink saucers over a lax mound, blooming through midsummer in ponderosa and aspen understory. Longer in flower than most natives here and comfortable in half a day of sun.
look: A lax, open mound of deeply cut, lobed green leaves, scattered with pink saucer-shaped flowers veined in magenta.

caution: Quinolizidine alkaloids throughout, concentrated in seed. Livestock-poisoning species; site away from grazing and do not plant where seed pods will be picked.
notes: Silver-silked foliage under blue-violet spikes, nitrogen-fixing and thoroughly adapted to lean mountain ground. Self-seeds into gaps, which is usually welcome in a naturalised planting.

Pink to white umbels nodding on a sharply bent stem, then holding as dried seed heads well into winter. Rated 10 by CSU. One of the most useful bulbs for high-elevation work — deer and elk leave alliums alone.

soil: Gritty, well-drained; tolerates seasonally moist ground
notes: Upright pink umbels, shorter and tidier than nodding onion and happy in ground that stays damp into early summer. Rated 10 by CSU.

soil: Lean, sharply drained; poor ground suits it
notes: Silver-grey stoloniferous mat with rose-tinted flower heads, host plant for American lady butterflies. Stoloniferous — it knits into a mat and will run between pavers and through low neighbours. Specify as matrix, path infill or erosion cover, not as a discrete drift.

soil: Moist but sharply drained; humus-rich in shade
caution: Cardiogenic toxins in foliage and seed, as in all columbines. Not for planting where seed will be gathered by children.
notes: The Colorado state flower — long-spurred blue and white, and the plant most clients at this elevation already want. Short-lived but self-seeds reliably into gravel and shaded gaps. Protected on public land; specify nursery stock, never collected.
look: A loose mound of rounded, lobed blue-green leaves under nodding flowers with long backswept spurs: sky-blue outer petals around a white cup.

notes: Compact blue-violet spikes over glossy evergreen basal rosettes that hold through winter — one of the few penstemons that reads as a groundcover out of bloom. Takes more shade than most of the genus.
look: Low clumps of glossy dark-green rosettes, with short upright spikes of small tubular blue-violet flowers.

soil: Sharply drained; rots in heavy wet soil
notes: Dense grassy evergreen tussock under pink globe flowers on wiry stems. Not native, but CSU-rated and a long-proven rock-garden plant at altitude — useful where a tidy evergreen cushion is wanted beside stone.
